analysis.one_liner: Bans electric utilities from charging residential customers payment fees beyond actual processing cost.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop electric utilities from charging customers extra payment fees has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since its August 2026 introduction, with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would pressure states to ban 'junk fees' that regulated electric utilities add to residential bills for ways of paying—like charging $3 or more to pay online or by phone. States would have to cap any payment fee at actual cost, provide at least one fee-free way to pay without internet access, ban fees on autopay and bank transfers, and give customers a way to recover illegally charged fees. If a state refuses, the Energy Department would withhold 10% of that state's federal energy program money until it complies.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential electricity customers, especially those who pay online or by phone and get hit with convenience fees that can cost the utility almost nothing to process. The bill would also help people who cannot easily use a website, by requiring a fee-free payment option that works without internet access.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Household electric customers paying utility junk fees

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps any payment fee at the greater of 150% of the utility's documented cost of processing the payment or $3, and bans fees on payment channels that cost the utility nothing, such as in-person payments, autopay, bank transfers, and mail payments [S2].

States must require utilities to disclose the fee amount, the reason for it, the total bill, and at least one fee-free payment option, and must give customers a way to recover unlawfully assessed fees through state enforcement [S2].
States that do not comply would lose 10% of their federal State Energy Program financial assistance, with a 90-day cure period and restoration of the money the following year if they comply [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Regulated electric utilities would lose fee revenue that currently exceeds their actual payment-processing costs, and the third-party payment processors they use would lose that business. States would face new compliance and enforcement duties tied to their federal energy grants.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism cuts federal money: a state that does not adopt these rules would lose 10% of its State Energy Program assistance, which funds state energy efficiency and planning work, so residents of a noncomplying state could see that program shrink [S2].

Utilities argue that payment fees recover real processing costs including interchange and fraud-prevention charges; while the bill excludes general overhead and profit from the allowable cost, utilities would bear the compliance burden of documenting costs and maintaining a fee-free offline payment channel [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the benefit is small in dollars per bill but real—fees on paying an electric bill are pure add-ons on a service people cannot go without. The main cost falls on utilities and their payment vendors, plus some state administrative work; the risk to the public is only if a state chooses to forgo 10% of its federal energy funds rather than adopt the fee rules, which would shrink state energy programs there.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Eugene Vindman introduced the bill on August 10, 2026 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action has been taken [S4].
No members have cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities keep collecting payment fees that exceed their processing costs, because the bill has gotten no traction in committee.

for.name: Eugene Vindman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, its sole sponsor

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred in August 2026

sides.party_line_note: There are no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Utilities currently charge residential customers payment fees that can far exceed their actual processing cost; the bill would cap or ban those fees and require a free offline payment option. Their fee revenue would drop, though they remain the sole provider of a service households cannot decline.

The bill's cost definition covers processor fees and interchange charges, and it requires utilities to offer fee-free channels such as autopay and bank transfers, shrinking the market for charging customers per transaction.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and two months of inactivity in the Energy and Commerce Committee, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027; first-term consumer-protection bills like this typically die in committee unless they attract broader support.
